'''Hans Ryde''' (born 17 January 1931) is a Swedish physicist who is a member of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]]. He was awarded his [[Doctor of Philosophy]] at Stockholm University in 1962.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Nuclear spectroscopic investigations on some selected radioactive decays: search för two-quantum transitions : studies on decays of deformed nuclei|last=Ryde|first=Hans|publisher=Univ.|year=1962|isbn=|location=Stockholm|pages=}}</ref> He was employed by the Research Institute of [[Atomic physics|Atomic Physics]] in [[Frescati (Stockholm)|Frescati]], [[Stockholm]] during the 60s and 70s, where he did his research in the field of [[Nuclear structure|nuclear structural physics]] in general and deformed nuclear nuclei in particular. By using a 225-cm [[cyclotron]] he discovered, together with his colleague Arne Johnson, that there was a backbending effect in fast rotating nuclei.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=A. |last2=Ryde |first2=H. |last3=Sztarkier |first3=J. |date=April 1971 |title=Evidence for a "singularity" in the nuclear rotational band structure |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/037026937190150X |journal=Physics Letters B |language=en |volume=34 |issue=7 |pages=605–608 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(71)90150-X|bibcode=1971PhLB...34..605J |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Chronicle of the discovery of the back-bending phenomenon in atomic nuclei: a personal recollection 50 years on|last=Ryde|first=Hans|journal=European Physical Journal H|publisher=Springer Nature|year=2021|volume=46|issue=1|page=23|doi=10.1140/epjh/s13129-021-00023-8|arxiv=2109.08144|bibcode=2021EPJH...46...23R|s2cid=237367555}}</ref> In 1975, he replaced [[Sten von Friesen]] as a [[professor]] at the Department of Physics, Lund University.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Fysik i Lund under 300 år|last=Litzén|first=Ulf|publisher=Lunds universitetshistoriska sällskap|year=2015|isbn=9789175453200|location=Lund|pages=129|language=Swedish}}</ref> He became a member of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]] in 1992<ref>{{Cite book|title=Matrikel|last=Kungl. Vetenskapsakademien|publisher=Kungl. Vetenskapsakademien|year=1964–2001|isbn=|location=Stockholm|pages=|language=Swedish}}</ref> and the [[Finnish Society of Sciences and Letters]] in 1988.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.scientiarum.fi/pdf/ledam%C3%B6ter/Utl%C3%A4ndska%20ledam%C3%B6ter_2017-01-02.pdf|title=Utländska ledamöter—Ulkomaiset jäsenet—Foreign Members|date=2017-01-02|website=scientiarum.fi|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170212091111/http://www.scientiarum.fi/pdf/ledam%C3%B6ter/Utl%C3%A4ndska%20ledam%C3%B6ter_2017-01-02.pdf|archive-date=2017-02-12|url-status=dead|access-date=2017-05-01}}</ref>

In 1972, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded Ryde the Edlund Prize "for work that led to the discovery of phase transitions in the atomic nucleus—the so-called nuclear Meissner effect", an early acknowledgement of the broader significance of the backbending phenomenon he had reported the previous year.<ref name="Edlund 1972"/>

Beyond research, he played a prominent international service role: during 1990–1993 he served as secretary of the Nuclear Physics Board of the [[European Physical Society]] (EPS), coordinating conference series such as "Nuclear Structure at High Spin" and helping to draft the EPS long-range plan for medium-energy accelerators.<ref name="EPS 1991"/>

During the late-1970s Ryde founded the [[Gamma spectroscopy|Gamma-Ray Spectroscopy]] Group at [[Lund]], securing funds for TESSA I, a 32-crystal [[germanium]] detector that was the largest high-resolution [[γ-ray]] array in Europe at the time. Its finer energy and timing precision let his team track how fast-spinning nuclei shed [[angular momentum]]: in medium-mass nuclei (around [[mass number]] 80) they followed a rotational sequence right up to the point where the spin can no longer be sustained, a limit known as band termination. With the same apparatus they observed that some heavier nuclei (mass number of about 150) adopt highly elongated "rugby-ball" shapes—so-called super-deformed bands—when rotating very rapidly. The two sets of results, published between 1983 and 1987, are now standard textbook cases of extreme nuclear motion.<ref name="Ryde 2021" />

Over the course of his career he supervised fifteen doctoral students, served on the editorial board of ''Nuclear Physics A'' (1986–1994) and, after formal retirement, helped integrate high-spin experiments into the [[MAX IV Laboratory|MAX-lab]] accelerator programme at Lund, acting as scientific adviser until 2005.<ref name="Litzén 2015p134" />
